Hard disk drives store data on spinning magnetic platters. They have been declared obsolete for most of two decades, steadily replaced in laptops and phones by flash memory with no moving parts. Seagate is one of only three companies that still makes them at scale. Its shares are up 206.48% over the past year, which is not how the story of a dying technology usually goes.

How Did Seagate (STX) Triple Selling a Technology Everyone Buried?
The Part Nobody Priced In:
Flash replaced hard drives where speed matters and size does not. It never replaced them where the opposite is true, which is storing enormous quantities of data that is rarely read.
Artificial intelligence produced exactly that kind of data, in volumes nobody had planned storage for. Hard drives remain considerably cheaper per unit of capacity, and at the scale data centres now operate, that difference decides the purchase.
The financial effect has been dramatic. Revenue rose 48.5% in the most recent quarter, and earnings grew 165.2%. Seagate holds one of the widest analyst gaps in our 10 Most Promising Technology Stocks to Buy Right Now. To see the rest, click HERE.
Three Companies and a Long Memory:
The pricing power comes from scarcity of supply rather than from anything special about the product. Three firms make these drives, and Seagate has told investors that the capacity it sells to data centres is fully allocated through this year. Demand arrived faster than the industry could serve it.
That is a condition rather than an advantage. Any competitor adding output changes it, and the industry has a long history of prices falling once supply catches up with demand. The balance sheet carries its own tension. Debt runs at 179.88% of equity, which is manageable while cash is flooding in and considerably less so if the pricing that produced it goes away.

A Cyclical Business at a Cyclical Price:
The shares change hands at 25.71 times what analysts expect next year, against 66.17 times the past year. The forward figure is the one the market is actually using, and it still assumes earnings stay far above where this business used to operate.
Everything rests on the shortage lasting. Judge that wrong and 25.71 times peak earnings turns into a far larger number on normal ones, which is the arithmetic that has caught buyers of this industry before.
Conclusion:
The technology was never finished, only pushed into the corner of the market where cost per unit of capacity beats speed. That corner then became the fastest-growing part of storage, which nobody forecast. The rise is real, and the reason for it is sound, but it rests on three companies having too little capacity rather than on anything a competitor cannot copy. Watch what any of them announces about building more, because that is the thing that ends this.

Hard drive demand has always moved in cycles. In fiscal 2023, Seagate lost $529 million. Data center sales now make up 80% of revenue, and that business leans on a few of hyperscalers whose spending could slow quickly.

The stock fell 9.19% over the past month and trades below its 50-day moving average of $855.24. It still holds above its 200-day average of $663.81.

At $753.25, Seagate trades well below the average analyst target.
Earnings are the path higher. Revenue grew 48.49% year over year last quarter, and GAAP gross margin expanded to 52.3% from 37.4%. Locked-in capacity means those gains rest on signed contracts.
The fiscal Q1 report is the next big catalyst. If Seagate meets its $7.30 EPS guide and confirms 2027 pricing, view could recover from the Toshiba shock. Over the next year, the shift to Mozaic 4 should push margins higher still.
Three things would break the thesis: hyperscaler order cuts, falling revenue per terabyte, or a HAMR yield setback. Seagate Technology Holdings now sits on a huge AI storage story and a share price that has already moved sharply. The real tension is whether that momentum still lines up with a sensible valuation.

On the narrative view, Seagate Technology Holdings is priced at $916.83 against an implied fair value of $1,158.73, which suggests the share price sits below where the story says it should be while also running far ahead of where it started this year.
Seagate is the storage-capacity position in a portfolio built on physical scarcity, and it''s the one I''d defend furthest into a downturn.
Not because the shortage is more durable than the others, it may or may not be. Because Seagate is the only one of my three storage holdings with a margin lever that runs independently of the pricing cycle.

The most followed storyline, according to isidrohg, rests on two moving parts that both matter for valuation. The first is a tight nearline HDD market where supply has not seen new capacity in roughly a decade. The second is the HAMR driven Mozaic platform, which is described as pushing areal density higher so that each exabyte shipped requires fewer physical components, lowering unit costs even if pricing conditions change.
In that framework, Seagate Technology Holdings is treated less like a simple pricing beneficiary and more like a business with its own internal cost curve. The narrative points to HAMR penetration moving from roughly 40% of nearline exabyte shipments toward a targeted 70% by June 2027, and links that shift directly to higher gross margins that are tied to technology mix rather than solely to contract prices.
Supporters of this view also highlight how that cost lever interacts with capital allocation and balance sheet choices. The emphasis on using recent free cash flow to cut debt, rather than pouring money into new greenfield capacity, is framed as a way to keep the current HDD duopoly tight, which in turn underpins the cash flow assumptions that feed into the fair value estimate of $1,158.73.

Still, Seagate Technology Holdings faces two clear pressure points: a potential HDD duopoly crack from new capacity and Western Digital closing the HAMR efficiency gap faster than expected.

At 65.5x earnings, the stock is far richer than both peers on 25.8x and the wider Tech group on 19.8x, and it also sits above an estimated fair ratio of 54.8x. That kind of gap points to real valuation risk if the growth story slips even modestly. The key question is which lens you trust more when the next wobble hits.

Flash replaced hard drives where speed matters and size does not. It never replaced them where the opposite is true, which is storing enormous quantities of data that is rarely read.
Artificial intelligence produced exactly that kind of data, in volumes nobody had planned storage for. Hard drives remain considerably cheaper per unit of capacity, and at the scale data centres now operate, that difference decides the purchase.

The pricing power comes from scarcity of supply rather than from anything special about the product. Three firms make these drives, and Seagate has told investors that the capacity it sells to data centres is fully allocated through this year. Demand arrived faster than the industry could serve it.
That is a condition rather than an advantage. Any competitor adding output changes it, and the industry has a long history of prices falling once supply catches up with demand. The balance sheet carries its own tension. Debt runs at 179.88% of equity, which is manageable while cash is flooding in and considerably less so if the pricing that produced it goes away.

The shares change hands at 25.71 times what analysts expect next year, against 66.17 times the past year. The forward figure is the one the market is actually using, and it still assumes earnings stay far above where this business used to operate.
Everything rests on the shortage lasting. Judge that wrong and 25.71 times peak earnings turns into a far larger number on normal ones, which is the arithmetic that has caught buyers of this industry before.

The technology was never finished, only pushed into the corner of the market where cost per unit of capacity beats speed. That corner then became the fastest-growing part of storage, which nobody forecast.
